Remember to continue to provide yourself daily motivation and encouragement towards your goals.

Questions: such as not enough sleep
I don't feel well.
Answers: It sounds like you're having a rough time, and it's okay to feel that way. Try to be gentle with yourself today: drink some water, eat something nourishing if you can, and take a few slow, deep breaths. If you're feeling unwell emotionally or physically and it persists or worsens, please reach out to a doctor or a trusted person. You deserve support and care.

Questions: I'm feeling anxious.
Answers: Anxiety is uncomfortable but common. Right now, try grounding yourself: notice 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell, and 1 you can taste. Then take slow breaths, breathing out longer than you breathe in. If anxiety keeps interfering with your daily life, a therapist can help you find strategies that work for you.

Questions: I can't sleep at night.
Answers: Poor sleep can make everything feel heavier. Try creating a wind-down routine: dim the lights an hour before bed, avoid screens, and keep your bedroom cool and quiet. If racing thoughts keep you awake, try writing them down before bed to get them out of your head. If insomnia continues for weeks, talk to your doctor, since sleep is important for your mental health.

Questions: I feel lonely.
Answers: Loneliness is painful, and it doesn't mean something is wrong with you. Reaching out counts, even in small ways: a message to a friend, a phone call, or joining an online community around something you enjoy. Connection is a skill that builds with practice. If the loneliness is deep and persistent, consider talking with a counselor who can support you.

Questions: I'm stressed about my exams.
Answers: Exam stress is real and manageable. Break your study into small, specific tasks and reward yourself for finishing each one. Take regular short breaks, move your body, and protect your sleep, especially the nights before exams. Remember that your worth is not your grades, and a few minutes of calm breathing can reset you between study sessions.

Questions: I feel overwhelmed.
Answers: Feeling overwhelmed usually means too much is on your plate. Pause and write down everything that's on your mind, then sort it: what truly must be done, what can wait, and what can be asked of others. Choose just one small next step and do it. You don't have to fix everything at once, and asking for help is a sign of strength, not weakness.

Questions: I have no motivation to do anything.
Answers: Loss of motivation can be a sign that you're running on empty, physically or emotionally. Start absurdly small: get out of bed, wash your face, step outside for two minutes. Small wins rebuild momentum better than big demands. If low motivation or low mood lasts more than two weeks, it's worth talking to a professional, because you don't have to carry it alone.

Questions: I keep overthinking everything.
Answers: Overthinking often gets worse when we try to force our minds to stop. Instead, give your thoughts a limit: write them down for 10 minutes, then gently redirect to a simple, absorbing task. Notice when your mind loops on 'what if' and label it as worry, not fact. If rumination is taking over your days, therapy can help you interrupt that cycle.

Questions: I feel worthless.
Answers: Thank you for telling me that. Feeling worthless is one of the hardest feelings, and I want you to know it's a feeling, not a fact about you. When it's this heavy, please don't face it alone: reach out to a trusted friend, a counselor, or a support line. You matter, and the people who love you would be glad you reached out.

Questions: I don't want to talk to anyone.
Answers: It's okay to need space, and it's also okay to set a low-pressure way to reconnect later, like a short text or a walk with someone you trust. Isolation can make heavy feelings heavier. If withdrawing is lasting a while and leaving you stuck, a therapist can be a safe, no-pressure person to start talking to.

Questions: I feel like crying.
Answers: Letting yourself cry is healthy; it's your body's way of releasing tension. Find somewhere safe and quiet, and let it out. Afterward, do something gentle for yourself, like a warm drink or a short walk. If the sadness feels constant or overwhelming, please talk to a doctor or counselor, and consider a support line if you need someone right now.

Questions: I'm angry all the time.
Answers: Anger is often a signal that a boundary has been crossed or a need isn't being met. Try to notice what triggers it, and practice pausing before reacting: take a breath, leave the room if you can, and move your body to release the energy. If anger is hurting your relationships, therapy can help you express it in ways that protect what you care about.

Questions: I'm worried about the future.
Answers: Worrying about the future is your mind trying to protect you, but it can spiral. Bring yourself back to what you can control today: one concrete plan, one small action, one moment of calm. Practice noticing when your thoughts turn to 'worst case' and gently reframe to 'most likely case.' Persistent worry is very treatable with the right support.

Questions: I can't focus.
Answers: Difficulty focusing often comes with stress, poor sleep, or feeling overwhelmed. Try one thing at a time, use a timer for short focus bursts with breaks, and reduce distractions like phone notifications. Check the basics too: sleep, food, and water. If focus problems are hurting your work or studies for weeks, mention it to your doctor, as it's worth understanding.

Questions: I feel like I'm not good enough.
Answers: Feeling 'not good enough' is extremely common and often louder than the evidence. Notice how you talk to yourself, and practice talking to yourself like you would a good friend. Reflect on things you've done that took effort, even small ones. If self-criticism is constant, therapy can help you soften that inner voice and build self-compassion.

Questions: I'm scared something bad is going to happen.
Answers: Fear is exhausting to carry. Grounding can help: plant your feet, feel the floor, and name five things you can see around you. Remind yourself that a scary feeling in your body is not the same as a true emergency. If fear or panic is frequent and intense, a therapist can teach you ways to respond to it that don't control your life.

Questions: I keep comparing myself to others.
Answers: Comparison is a trap, because you see others' highlights and your own outtakes. Limit the triggers: unfollow accounts that make you feel small, and notice what you're grateful for in your own life instead. Practice celebrating small personal wins. Remember that everyone's path is different, and yours is not behind, it's just yours.

Questions: I feel numb.
Answers: Feeling numb can be your mind's way of protecting you from something overwhelming. Be gentle with yourself, and try small sensory comforts: warm showers, soft music, time in nature. Slowly reconnecting with your body can help feelings return safely. If numbness lasts a long time or follows something painful, please reach out for professional support.

Questions: I'm dreading going to work.
Answers: Dreading work can point to burnout, stress, or a mismatch that deserves attention. Protect your rest, set boundaries on overtime, and build small breaks into your day. It's also worth reflecting on what's draining you and whether changes or a conversation with your manager are possible. If work stress is taking over your wellbeing, talking to a counselor can help you sort it out.

Questions: I feel so much pressure.
Answers: Pressure can be external or something we put on ourselves. Try lowering the bar in one area today and see what happens. Name the expectations you're carrying and ask which are truly yours. Share the load where you can, and make time for recovery, because rest is not a reward for finishing everything, it's part of how you keep going.

Questions: I keep having bad memories.
Answers: Intrusive memories can be very distressing. Grounding helps bring you back to the present: touch something with texture, press your feet into the floor, say today's date and place out loud. Try not to fight the memory, but let it pass like a cloud while you stay in the here and now. If memories are re-traumatizing you, please reach out to a professional, because trauma therapy can genuinely help.

Questions: I feel guilty all the time.
Answers: Guilt can be heavy even when it's undeserved. Ask yourself: did I truly do something wrong, or am I holding myself to an impossible standard? If you did hurt someone, repair is possible with an honest apology and changed behavior. If the guilt is persistent and tied to old events, therapy can help you work through it and forgive yourself.

Questions: I'm scared of failing.
Answers: Fear of failure often comes from tying your worth to results. Try to separate the two: you are worthy regardless of outcomes. Shift your goal from 'don't fail' to 'learn something,' and notice that most failures are reversible or smaller than they felt. Sharing your fear with someone you trust can shrink it, too.

Questions: I feel empty.
Answers: Feeling empty can be unsettling. Gently bring yourself into the present with your senses, and try small activities that give you a feeling of accomplishment, even tiny ones. Sometimes emptiness is a signal that a need or feeling is being pushed down. If it persists or deepens, talking to a professional can help you explore what's underneath it.

Questions: I'm struggling to get out of bed.
Answers: That sounds really hard, and I'm glad you're talking about it. Try shrinking the task: sit up, then stand, then make your bed or splash water on your face. One tiny action often loosens the grip. If every morning feels like a battle for weeks, please see a doctor or counselor, because low energy and low mood can be treated.

Questions: I feel like a burden to others.
Answers: You are not a burden, even when it feels that way. People who care about you want to be there for you, and your needs matter as much as anyone's. If the feeling of being a burden is strong and constant, please reach out to a professional or a support line today, because you deserve to be heard and helped.

Questions: I'm having a panic attack.
Answers: If you're having a panic attack right now, try this: breathe in through your nose for 4 seconds, hold for 4, out through your mouth for 6, and repeat a few times. Remind yourself that panic attacks are frightening but not dangerous and they pass. Find a safe place and ground yourself in the present. If they keep happening, a therapist can help you break the pattern.

Questions: I don't enjoy things anymore.
Answers: Losing interest in things you used to love is a common sign of depression and it's very treatable. Try reconnecting in small doses without pressure to enjoy it, and notice what tiny moments feel even slightly good. Be kind to yourself about it. Please consider talking to a doctor or counselor, because this kind of heaviness lifts with the right support.

Questions: I'm procrastinating everything.
Answers: Procrastination is usually avoidance of a big, vague task. Make the task smaller and concrete, decide the very next physical action, and use a 5-minute timer to start. Reward yourself for starting, not for finishing. Lowering the stakes of starting is often enough to break the freeze and get you moving.

Questions: I keep fighting with my partner.
Answers: Conflict in close relationships is normal, but constant fighting hurts both of you. Try pausing before responding, using 'I feel' statements instead of accusations, and taking a break to cool down when emotions are high. A calm conversation later is more productive than a heated one now. Couples counseling can help if the pattern is stuck.

Questions: I feel hopeless.
Answers: Thank you for being honest with me. Hopelessness is one of the heaviest feelings, and it's important that you don't sit with it alone. Please reach out to someone you trust right now, call a crisis or support line, and consider speaking with a doctor or therapist. Your situation can change, and people can help you see a way through that you can't see right now.

Questions: I'm drinking too much lately.
Answers: Thank you for being honest about that. Alcohol can seem to dull heavy feelings but often makes them worse over time. Try tracking your drinking, setting a clear limit, and finding alternatives for the moments you reach for it. If you're drinking to cope with emotional pain, talking to a professional can help address the root cause. And please, never stop drinking cold turkey if you've been drinking heavily; get medical help to do it safely.

Questions: I'm scared to go outside.
Answers: Being afraid to go outside can be overwhelming and isolating. Start very small: stand at the door for a minute, then a short walk, then a little further, and praise each step. Take someone you trust with you at first. If going out is consistently terrifying, a therapist can help you work through the fear gradually and safely.

Questions: I feel like nobody understands me.
Answers: Feeling misunderstood is deeply lonely. Try expressing what you're going through in a way that helps others meet you, and it's okay if it takes a few tries to feel heard. Connecting with people who share your experiences, like support groups, can help a lot. A therapist's job is to understand you without judgment.

Questions: I'm not ready to forgive myself.
Answers: Forgiveness, especially of yourself, is not something you owe anyone on a timeline. Start with acknowledging what happened and what you learned, and treat yourself with the compassion you'd give a friend in the same situation. Healing is often a gradual process, and it's okay to take it slowly. A counselor can walk with you through it.

Questions: I feel so tired all the time.
Answers: Constant tiredness can come from stress, poor sleep, low mood, or physical causes. Protect your sleep schedule, stay hydrated, and get gentle movement. Also consider whether emotional load is draining you. If tiredness lasts more than a few weeks, see a doctor, because it's worth checking both physical and mental health.

Questions: I'm scared of being alone.
Answers: Being afraid of being alone is common and understandable. Build small anchors in your day: a regular check-in with a friend, a community or class, or a pet if that suits you. Practice short stretches of being alone with something comforting, and notice what you enjoy in your own company. If the fear is intense, talking to a therapist can help.

Questions: I don't know how to relax.
Answers: Relaxation is a skill that needs practice, not a switch. Try progressive muscle relaxation: tense each muscle group for a few seconds, then let go, from your feet to your face. Or try slow breathing, gentle stretching, or listening to music without other distractions. Give yourself permission to practice, and it gets easier.

Questions: I feel like everything is my fault.
Answers: Blaming yourself for everything is exhausting and usually not accurate. When you notice self-blame, ask: what else could have contributed here, and what would I say to a friend in my shoes? Practicing that question helps balance the picture. If you're stuck in harsh self-blame, a therapist can help you untangle it.

Questions: I'm worried about my family.
Answers: Caring about family is a strength, but constant worry about them can drain you. Separate what you can influence from what you can't, and act only on the first. You can support your family without carrying their problems alone. Talking about your worries with someone you trust, or a counselor, can help you hold the care without the exhaustion.

Questions: I feel like I'm failing at life.
Answers: That feeling is more common than you think, and it's usually not an accurate summary of who you are. Make a list of things you've handled, even small ones, and read it when the feeling is loud. Life is long and nonlinear, and this chapter does not decide the whole story. If the feeling is heavy and constant, please reach out for professional support.

Questions: I can't let go of the past.
Answers: Letting go is rarely a single decision; it's a practice. Try writing about what happened, what you learned, and what you might need to move forward. Gently remind yourself that revisiting the past doesn't change it, while planning your present does. If the past is holding you hostage, trauma-informed therapy can help you find real release.

Questions: I feel anxious about my health.
Answers: Health anxiety can spiral quickly, with every symptom feeding worry. Limit checking and googling symptoms, and bring specific concerns to a doctor once rather than endlessly searching. Practice grounding when the worry spikes. If health anxiety is taking over your days, cognitive behavioral therapy is very effective for it.

Questions: I have no friends.
Answers: Having no friends right now is painful, and friendship is a skill that can be rebuilt. Start with low-stakes connection: a class, a hobby group, volunteering, or an online community around an interest. Focus on showing up consistently rather than waiting for instant closeness. A therapist or support group can also be a safe place to practice connection.

Questions: I feel like giving up.
Answers: Please stop and read this: you matter, and your life is worth fighting for, even when it doesn't feel that way. Right now, reach out to someone you trust, call a crisis or support line in your country, or go to an emergency room if you're in immediate danger. You don't have to fix everything today, you just have to reach for help. People can and will help you find a way through.

Questions: I can't stop worrying about money.
Answers: Money worries are heavy and very common. Start by getting a clear picture: list what's coming in and going out, and tackle one small action, like a budget or one bill. Separate what you can control now from what you can't. Financial stress often feels private, but talking about it with someone trusted can lighten it, and free financial advice services exist to help.

Questions: I don't feel like myself anymore.
Answers: Feeling unlike yourself is unsettling, and it's a real signal worth honoring. Check the basics first: sleep, food, stress, and whether something big has shifted in your life. Give yourself grace while you adjust. If this feeling lasts for weeks or comes with low mood, please talk to a doctor or counselor, because finding your way back to yourself is very possible with support.

Questions: I'm scared to talk about my feelings.
Answers: It's very common to be scared of opening up, especially if it wasn't safe to before. Start small: share a little with one trusted person, or write it out first. Notice that being vulnerable is a risk, but isolation is a bigger one. A therapist is a good place to practice, because they're trained to receive whatever you bring without judgment.

Questions: I keep thinking the worst.
Answers: The worst-case imagination is a habit that can be softened. When you catch it, ask: what is the most likely outcome, and what is the best realistic outcome? Write down evidence for a less catastrophic view. Practicing this regularly rewires the habit over time. If catastrophic thinking is constant and distressing, therapy can help you rebalance it.

Questions: I feel sad for no reason.
Answers: Sadness that shows up without an obvious reason can be confusing. Be gentle with yourself, and check in on the basics: sleep, food, and how long you've been carrying stress. Sometimes feelings arrive late or quietly. If the sadness is lasting or getting heavier, talking to a doctor or counselor is a strong, caring step, not a sign of weakness.

Questions: I'm struggling after a breakup.
Answers: Breakups hurt, and the grief is real. Allow yourself to feel it without judging the timeline. Remove constant reminders of your ex, lean on trusted friends, and rebuild small routines that are just yours. Grief comes in waves, so expect good days and hard days. If the pain is crushing or lasting a long time, counseling can help you heal.

Questions: I feel like I have to be perfect.
Answers: Perfectionism is exhausting and rooted in fear of judgment. Try deliberately doing something 'good enough' and notice the world doesn't end. Replace 'I must be perfect' with 'I can be human.' Reflect on what perfectionism is protecting you from, and practice showing yourself the same kindness you show others. Progress is more sustainable than perfection.

Questions: I'm scared of people judging me.
Answers: Feeling judged often says more about our own self-criticism than about others' actual thoughts. Notice the evidence for and against your assumption. Most people are absorbed in their own lives. Practice acting naturally in small situations and let real reactions, not imagined ones, be your guide. Building self-acceptance makes imagined judgment fade.

Questions: How can I calm down quickly?
Answers: Try this: breathe in through your nose for 4 seconds, hold for 4, and exhale slowly through your mouth for 6 seconds, a few times. Then ground yourself with your senses, naming things you can see, touch, hear, smell, and taste. Slow exhales tell your nervous system it's safe, and the panic settles faster than you'd expect.

Questions: How do I handle a panic attack?
Answers: If a panic attack is happening, remind yourself it's frightening but not dangerous, and it will pass. Use slow breathing: in for 4, hold for 4, out for 6. Splash cold water on your face or hold something with texture to ground yourself. Afterward, rest and be kind to yourself. If they happen often, a therapist can help you break the pattern.

Questions: What are good grounding techniques?
Answers: The 5-4-3-2-1 technique is a great start: name five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, and one you can taste. You can also press your feet into the floor, hold an ice cube, or describe the room in detail. These bring your attention back to the present when your mind is spinning.

Questions: How can I stop negative thoughts?
Answers: You can't switch thoughts off, but you can change how you relate to them. Label the thought as 'just a thought, not a fact' and let it pass like a cloud. Ask yourself what you'd tell a friend having the same thought. Write it down to get it outside your head. If negative thinking is constant, therapy can teach you to challenge it effectively.

Questions: How do I build a morning routine that helps my mood?
Answers: Keep it small and consistent: wake around the same time, get light into your eyes early, drink water, and move your body for a few minutes. Add one thing you look forward to, like a favorite drink or a few pages of a book. A gentle, repeatable morning gives you stability, which quietly supports your mental health.

Questions: How can I improve my sleep?
Answers: Protect a consistent sleep schedule, even on weekends. Wind down for an hour before bed: dim lights, avoid screens, and keep the room cool and quiet. If your mind races, keep a notebook by the bed and write thoughts down. Avoid caffeine late in the day. If insomnia lasts weeks, talk to your doctor, because sleep is foundational to mood.

Questions: What are good breathing exercises?
Answers: Box breathing is simple and effective: breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4, and repeat. Another is the 4-6 exhale: breathe in for 4 and out slowly for 6. Longer exhales calm the nervous system fastest. Even a couple of minutes of slow breathing can lower your stress noticeably.

Questions: How do I stop overthinking?
Answers: Give worry a time limit: write everything down for 10 minutes, then close the notebook and redirect to a simple, absorbing task. Catch 'what if' loops and label them as worry, not facts. Overthinking feeds on trying to stop it, so gently moving attention helps more than fighting it. If it's constant, therapy can help you interrupt the cycle.

Questions: How can I feel better when I'm sad?
Answers: Let yourself feel the sadness without judging it; it's information, not weakness. Then do something gentle: a warm shower, a walk outside, a call to someone you trust, or listening to music you love. Small actions and connection lift mood gradually. If sadness is heavy or lasting, please talk to a professional, because support genuinely helps.

Questions: What should I do when I feel overwhelmed?
Answers: Stop and write everything down to get it out of your head. Sort it into what must happen now, what can wait, and what can be shared or dropped. Choose one small next step and do only that. Then protect rest. Overwhelm shrinks when the invisible load becomes a visible list, and you don't have to do it all at once.

Questions: How can I manage stress from work?
Answers: Set a clear end to your workday and create a ritual that marks it, like a walk or changing clothes. Protect breaks during the day and use them to actually rest. Talk to your manager about realistic priorities if the load is unsustainable. If work stress is constant, burnout support and counseling can help you reset.

Questions: What are some coping strategies for anxiety?
Answers: Anxiety responds well to grounding, slow breathing, and breaking tasks into tiny steps. Movement helps burn off the extra energy anxiety creates. Limit caffeine and check your sleep, since both feed anxiety. Identify your triggers and plan for them. If anxiety is frequent, cognitive behavioral therapy is highly effective at building lasting coping skills.

Questions: How do I talk to someone about how I feel?
Answers: Start with one person you trust, and use simple words: 'I've been struggling lately' or 'I need to talk about something heavy.' You don't have to explain everything at once. You can ask for what you need, like listening rather than advice. Practicing on a safe person builds the skill, and a therapist is a good place to practice too.

Questions: How can I help a friend who is struggling?
Answers: Be present and listen without rushing to fix things. Ask open questions and reflect what you hear, like 'that sounds really hard.' Offer specific, low-pressure support, such as going for a walk or checking in tomorrow. Take their mental health seriously and gently encourage professional help when needed, and take care of yourself too.

Questions: How do I get motivated again?
Answers: Start with something absurdly small, because action creates motivation rather than the other way around. Make the first step tiny: put on your shoes, open the document, take out the ingredients. Reward yourself for starting, not finishing. Protect sleep and movement, since energy drives motivation. If low motivation lasts, it may be depression, which is treatable.

Questions: What are good habits for mental health?
Answers: Sleep, movement, and connection are the foundations. Regular sleep and some physical activity each day lift mood. Keep real social contact, even brief. Add small daily rituals: time outside, a hobby, a moment of gratitude. Practice noticing when you need rest. These habits don't fix everything, but they make everything else more possible.

Questions: How can I stop comparing myself to others?
Answers: Comparison is a habit you can interrupt. Curate your feeds so you see fewer highlight reels, and notice what you're grateful for in your own life. Measure yourself against your own past, not others' milestones. Practice celebrating others' wins without measuring yourself against them. Over time, self-focus replaces comparison.

Questions: How do I set healthy boundaries?
Answers: Start small and use a simple, kind script like 'I can't take that on right now.' You don't need to over-explain. Notice that people usually adapt to clear limits, and relationships often improve with honesty. Each boundary protects something you value. Boundaries are a skill, and they get easier with practice.

Questions: What helps with loneliness?
Answers: Small, consistent connection beats rare big gestures. Reach out with a low-pressure message or call, and join something recurring where you see the same faces, like a class or group. Loneliness is eased by being known over time, so show up regularly. If loneliness is deep, a support group or counselor can help you rebuild connection.

Questions: How can I deal with anger in a healthy way?
Answers: Pause before reacting, and use an exit: take a breath, step away, or count to ten. Move your body to discharge the energy, like a brisk walk. Name what the anger is protecting, whether it's a boundary or a need, and address that directly with 'I feel' statements. If anger is hurting relationships, therapy can help you channel it.

Questions: What should I do when I feel like giving up?
Answers: Please reach out for help right now. Contact a trusted person, call a crisis or support line in your country, or go to an emergency room if you're in immediate danger. You don't have to solve everything today, just take the step of telling someone. There is support for you, and things can get better with help.

Questions: How can I practice self-compassion?
Answers: Speak to yourself the way you'd speak to a friend who was struggling. When you make a mistake, acknowledge it without attacking yourself. Give yourself credit for effort, and allow imperfection. Notice your harsh inner voice and gently rewrite it. Self-compassion is a practice that grows with repetition, and it genuinely changes how you feel.

Questions: How do I handle difficult emotions?
Answers: Start by naming the emotion, which calms the brain. Let the feeling be present without acting on it, like weather passing through. Use slow breathing and grounding when it's intense. Ask what the emotion is telling you about your needs. Over time this builds emotional capacity, and therapy can give you more tools if needed.

Questions: What helps with grief?
Answers: Grief has no timeline, so allow yourself the waves. Talk about the person you lost with people who listen, and honor them in small ways. Let others help you with practical things while you grieve. Over time, the pain softens and the love remains. If grief feels impossible to carry, grief counseling can genuinely help.

Questions: How can I build confidence?
Answers: Confidence grows from evidence, so collect it: note small things you did well, and set tiny achievable goals you actually complete. Practice skills in low-stakes settings before big ones. Notice your self-talk and challenge it like you'd defend a friend. Confidence is built one kept promise to yourself at a time.

Questions: What are some ways to relax my mind?
Answers: Try slow, extended exhales, which calm the nervous system. Give your mind a single focus, like the breath or a word, and let thoughts pass without chasing them. Try a short guided relaxation or gentle stretching. Don't force quiet; just practice returning attention gently. Mental rest is a skill that improves with regular practice.

Questions: How do I stop feeling so tired all the time?
Answers: Protect your sleep schedule, stay hydrated, and get gentle daily movement, which often boosts energy. Look at your stress load, since emotional load drains you physically. If tiredness persists for weeks, see a doctor to check for physical causes like anemia or thyroid issues, as well as mental health factors like depression.

Questions: How can I deal with work stress?
Answers: Set boundaries around your hours and protect breaks that actually let you rest. Prioritize tasks and learn to say no to non-essential demands. Move your body and get outside during the day. If the stress is constant, talk to your manager about the load and consider whether burnout support is needed. Your wellbeing comes first.

Questions: What helps when I'm feeling overwhelmed with everything?
Answers: Externalize the load: write it all down, then sort into 'now,' 'later,' and 'not mine to carry.' Act only on 'now.' Delegate or drop what you can. Protect rest like it's part of the work. You don't have to carry everything alone, and asking for help is a practical strategy, not a failure.

Questions: How can I sleep when my mind won't stop?
Answers: Keep a notepad by your bed and write down racing thoughts to get them out of your head. Try slow breathing in bed, exhaling longer than you inhale. Keep the room dark, cool, and quiet, and avoid screens for an hour before bed. If your mind is racing from stress, address the stress in the daytime with exercise and talk.

Questions: How do I stop worrying so much?
Answers: Give worry a container: set aside 15 minutes a day as 'worry time,' and defer worries to it. Write worries down and sort them into what you can act on and what you can't. Act on the first, release the second. Worry thrives on endless replay; time-boxing and writing break that loop. If worry is constant, therapy can help.

Questions: How can I handle criticism without falling apart?
Answers: Separate the useful signal from the tone. If there's a kernel of truth, take it and let go of the harsh delivery. Thank the person briefly and take time to consider rather than reacting in the moment. Remind yourself your worth isn't decided by one critique. You can learn from feedback without accepting every judgment.

Questions: What should I do when I don't want to get out of bed?
Answers: Shrink the task: just sit up, then stand, then splash water on your face or make your bed. One tiny action loosens the grip of inertia. Make your morning gentle, with light and one small pleasant thing. If this lasts more than two weeks, please talk to a doctor or counselor, because low energy and low mood can be treated.

Questions: How can I be kinder to myself?
Answers: Notice your harsh self-talk and rewrite it as you'd speak to a good friend. Give yourself credit for effort, not just results. Allow mistakes without self-attack, and practice saying something kind to yourself each day. Self-kindness is a habit, and like any habit, it strengthens with repetition and genuinely changes how you experience life.

Questions: What helps with social anxiety?
Answers: Practice in small, low-stakes steps: a brief chat with a cashier, asking a question in a group, then longer interactions. Prepare a few open questions so you're not stuck for words. Remember most people are focused on themselves. Each small step builds evidence that socializing is survivable. If it's severe, therapy, especially exposure work, helps a lot.

Questions: How do I stop feeling guilty all the time?
Answers: Ask whether the guilt fits the facts: did you actually do wrong, or are you holding yourself to an impossible standard? If you hurt someone, repair with an honest apology and changed behavior, then let it go. Guilt is meant to correct course, not to become your identity. If it's tied to old events, therapy can help you work through it.

Questions: How can I get through a really hard day?
Answers: Break the day into small chunks and handle only the current one: one meal, one task, one breath at a time. Reach out to someone you trust, even briefly. Let go of what can wait, and be gentle about what didn't get done. You don't have to feel good to keep going, and asking for help makes hard days lighter.

Questions: What are quick ways to reduce stress?
Answers: Take three slow, extended exhales, which calm the nervous system immediately. Step outside for a minute of daylight and fresh air. Splash cold water on your face or hold something cold. Do a quick body scan, relaxing your shoulders and jaw. Small resets like these are practical tools you can use anywhere, anytime.

Questions: How can I stop procrastinating?
Answers: Procrastination is usually avoidance of a big, vague task. Make the task tiny and concrete, decide the next physical action, and start a 5-minute timer. Reward yourself for starting, not finishing. Lower the stakes of starting and the freeze usually breaks. If procrastination is chronic, it may be tied to anxiety or perfectionism worth addressing.

Questions: How do I handle feeling not good enough?
Answers: Notice how you talk to yourself and challenge the harsh voice like you'd defend a friend. Write down evidence of things you've done that took effort, even small ones. Comparison feeds 'not good enough,' so limit it. Your worth isn't a performance. If self-criticism is constant, therapy can help you build a fairer, kinder inner voice.

Questions: What helps with rumination and repetitive thoughts?
Answers: Gently interrupt the loop: name it ('this is rumination') and shift attention to a simple, absorbing task or your senses. Give the thought a time limit and write it down rather than replaying it. Worry about the same thing repeatedly rarely changes anything; action or acceptance do. If rumination dominates, cognitive behavioral therapy can break the cycle.

Questions: How can I rebuild after a mistake?
Answers: Acknowledge the mistake honestly without global self-blame: you are not your worst moment. Extract the lesson and decide what you'd do differently. Make amends if someone was hurt, then consciously choose to move forward. Mistakes are data, not verdicts. If you're stuck replaying it, writing or therapy can help you release it.

Questions: What should I do if I'm worried about my mental health?
Answers: Worried is actually a good first step, because it means you're aware and ready to act. Start by speaking with a professional who can help you understand what you're experiencing, whether a doctor, counselor, or support line. You don't need a crisis to get help. Your mind deserves the same care your body does.

Questions: How do I practice mindfulness?
Answers: Mindfulness is simple attention to the present. Sit comfortably and focus on your breath, and when your mind wanders, gently return to it without judgment. Or do a walking meditation, noticing each step and your surroundings. Even a few minutes a day builds the skill. It's called a practice because you keep practicing returning to now.

Questions: What helps when I feel invisible or unappreciated?
Answers: Start by acknowledging yourself: keep a small list of things you did that mattered today. Then communicate your needs directly, because people often don't notice what isn't said. Notice where your contributions genuinely land and invest there. You deserve to be seen, and sometimes that starts with seeing yourself and asking clearly.

Questions: How can I deal with feeling trapped in my situation?
Answers: Make a list of every option you can see, however small, and choose one action you can take this week. Talk to someone who can help you see choices you can't. Very few situations are truly without doors, and you don't have to find your way out alone. A counselor can help you map a path and take the first step.

Questions: What helps with self-doubt?
Answers: Collect evidence: write down things you've done well and challenges you've handled. Notice when your self-doubt is loudest and what triggers it. Take small actions anyway, since action builds confidence better than waiting to feel sure. Compare yourself to your own past, not others. If self-doubt is deep, therapy can help you uncover its roots.

Questions: How can I make better use of my time?
Answers: Start by noticing where your time actually goes for a couple of days. Protect the hours that matter most, and say no to what doesn't serve you. Batch small tasks and give hard tasks your freshest energy. Rest is not wasted time; it's what makes the rest possible. You're not behind on living, you're just planning it.

Questions: What should I do when I feel like I can't cope?
Answers: That feeling is a signal that you need more support, not a sign of failure. Tell someone you trust today, and consider speaking with a professional or a support line. Break the immediate load into one small step. You don't have to cope alone; help genuinely lightens this, even when it feels impossible. Please reach out.

Questions: How do I stop feeling like a burden?
Answers: You are not a burden; that's shame talking. People who love you want to be there for you, and your needs are legitimate. Try asking for something small and specific and notice how it's received, which often disproves the feeling. If it's heavy and constant, talk to a professional today, because you deserve to be heard and helped.

Questions: How can I feel more connected to people?
Answers: Connection grows from repeated, low-pressure contact. Join something recurring where you see the same faces, ask people real questions, and share small things about yourself. You don't need deep conversations immediately; consistency builds trust. If you've been isolated, start small and let it build. Connection is a skill, and it can be rebuilt.

Questions: What helps me when I feel anxious about the future?
Answers: Bring yourself back to what you can control today: one plan, one action, one calm moment. Write down your concerns and sort them into 'can act' and 'can't control,' and act only on the first. Remind yourself you've survived uncertain times before. Persistent future worry is very treatable with the right support.

Questions: How can I deal with feeling not smart enough?
Answers: Intelligence is diverse and practical, emotional, and creative, not just academic. Make a list of things you're genuinely good at, however humble. Learning is a skill that grows with practice, so focus on one small improvement. 'Not smart enough' is a story, not a fact, and your worth was never based on it anyway.

Questions: What should I do when I don't want to talk to anyone?
Answers: It's okay to need space; give yourself a set amount of it. Then set a low-pressure way to reconnect, like a short text or a walk with someone you trust. Isolation makes heavy feelings heavier, so small contact helps more than it seems. If withdrawing is lasting and leaving you stuck, a therapist is a safe, no-pressure person to start talking to.

Questions: How can I stop feeling empty?
Answers: Gently bring yourself into the present with your senses, and try small activities that give you a sense of accomplishment, even tiny ones. Sometimes emptiness is a signal that a need or feeling is being pushed down, so give it room to surface. If it persists or deepens, talking to a professional can help you explore what's underneath.

Questions: What helps with feeling like nothing is worth it?
Answers: That feeling is one of the heaviest, and it's important you don't sit with it alone. Please reach out to someone you trust or a support line today. Hopelessness feels permanent but it can lift with the right support; depression is treatable and people do find their way through. You deserve that chance, and help is available.

Questions: How can I stop being so hard on myself?
Answers: Catch the critical thought and ask how you'd respond to a friend who said it. Replace harsh judgments with fair, kind ones. Give yourself credit for effort, and allow mistakes without self-attack. Notice the difference between holding yourself accountable and attacking yourself. Self-compassion is a skill that grows with practice, and it changes everything.

Questions: What do I do when I keep reliving the past?
Answers: When the past replays, ground yourself: feet on the floor, slow breathing, name what's around you. Remind yourself the moment is over and you're safe now. Writing about it, especially with professional guidance if it's trauma, can help move it into the past where it belongs. You deserve relief from the replay.

Questions: How can I feel less lonely during the holidays?
Answers: Plan something gentle for yourself: a favorite meal, a walk, a call to someone you know. Reach out to others who may also be alone; you're often not the only one. You can create meaning even when traditions look different. Holiday loneliness doesn't mean you're unlovable; it means the season is hard, and it's okay to meet it with care.

Questions: How can I learn to trust others again?
Answers: Rebuild trust in small doses: share something small with someone consistent and notice how they handle it. Trust is built through repeated, safe experiences, not through big leaps. Notice the difference between old betrayals and present people. If past hurts are deep, therapy can help you heal them so new relationships have a fair chance.

Questions: What helps me when I feel like I have no purpose?
Answers: Purpose is built, not discovered all at once. Notice what gives you moments of meaning: helping someone, learning, creating, connecting. Invest in those, even in small ways. Purpose can change across life stages, and that's okay. You don't need one grand purpose; you need threads of meaning, and they're already in your life.

Questions: How can I deal with feeling behind in life?
Answers: Feeling behind is a comparison to others' visible milestones, not an objective fact. Life is long and nonlinear; quiet phases often build foundations. Focus on your own direction and recent progress. Speed is not a measure of worth. You're not behind, you're on your own route, and it's valid.

Questions: What helps when I feel like people won't understand me?
Answers: Understanding is often built, not assumed. Express yourself clearly and give people a chance to meet you, and find listeners who make an effort. Some won't understand, and that's about their capacity, not your worth. A therapist is someone trained to understand you without judgment. You deserve to be heard.

Questions: How can I handle feeling overwhelmed by my thoughts?
Answers: Write your thoughts down to externalize them, then sort them into what needs action and what's just noise. Practice grounding to return to your body and the present. Create more quiet in your life: fewer inputs, more stillness. If thoughts are relentless, professional support can help you build calm. A quieter mind is possible, and it's worth working toward.

Questions: What do I do when I feel like I can't go on?
Answers: Please reach out for help right now. Contact someone you trust, call a crisis or support line in your country, or go to an emergency room if you're in immediate danger. You don't have to fix everything today, just tell someone how you're feeling. People can and will help you find a way through, and this feeling can change with support.

Questions: How can I be okay with being alone?
Answers: Build a life you enjoy: interests, routines, and a space that feels like yours. Learn what you love and make time for it. Being alone isn't the same as being lonely, and your own company can become a comfort. Start with short, gentle stretches of solitude and notice what you enjoy. If being alone is heavy, therapy can help you build a kinder relationship with yourself.

Questions: What helps with feeling like I'm always worried?
Answers: Constant worry keeps your nervous system on alert. Give worry a daily container, write concerns down, and sort them into what you can act on and what you can't. Protect rest and movement, since they calm the baseline. If worry is your constant companion, cognitive behavioral therapy is highly effective at loosening its grip.

Questions: How can I deal with my partner's mood?
Answers: Start by caring for your own wellbeing and boundaries; you can support your partner without absorbing their mood. Ask what they need, and offer calm presence rather than trying to fix everything. Encourage professional support if their mood is persistent. Relationships weather storms better when both people take care of themselves too.

Questions: What should I do when I feel numb?
Answers: Numbness is often your mind's way of protecting you from overwhelm. Be gentle with yourself and try small sensory comforts: warm showers, soft music, time in nature. Slowly reconnecting with your body can help feelings return safely. If numbness lasts a long time or follows something painful, please reach out for professional support.

Questions: How can I feel more optimistic?
Answers: Optimism is a skill you can build by noticing what's going well, however small, and by balancing worst-case thinking with most-likely and best-case thinking. Act on what you can control and release the rest. Hope grows with evidence, so collect it. If hopelessness is persistent, professional support can help you find your way back to it.

Questions: What helps with feeling of being judged at work?
Answers: Focus on what you can control: doing solid work, asking for feedback, and learning from it. Feedback is about the work, not your worth. Notice when the imagined judgment doesn't show up, and let evidence correct the fear. If work anxiety is intense, therapy can help you build confidence and separate real signals from imagined ones.

Questions: How do I build emotional resilience?
Answers: Resilience is built through small, repeated supports: protecting sleep, staying connected, practicing self-compassion, and facing challenges in manageable steps. Notice what's helped you through past hard times and use those tools. Resilience isn't a fixed trait; it grows as you recover, rest, and learn. Support from others makes it stronger.

Questions: What should I do if I keep having bad dreams?
Answers: Bad dreams often reflect stress or difficult experiences. Wind down calmly before bed, reduce scary content before sleep, and write out daytime worries earlier. Protect your sleep routine and make your bedroom feel safe. If nightmares are frequent and distressing, professional help, including trauma-informed therapy, can genuinely reduce them.

Questions: How can I stop feeling jealous of others?
Answers: Jealousy is a signal pointing at something you want for yourself. Name it, then take one small step toward your own version. Practice gratitude for what you already have. Envy thrives on comparison and starves on self-focus. With practice, jealousy becomes a prompt for growth rather than a source of pain.

Questions: What helps when I feel disconnected from my body?
Answers: Try slow, gentle activities that bring you into your body: stretching, walking, warm showers, or noticing your breath. Move without performance pressure. Reconnecting takes time and gentleness, so go at your own pace. If the disconnection is strong or linked to trauma, professional support can help you reconnect safely.

Questions: How can I deal with feeling like I'm always on edge?
Answers: Being on edge often means your nervous system is carrying too much. Build in rest, slow breathing, and gentle movement, and reduce stressors where you can. Notice what keeps you on alert and address it directly. If constant tension is your baseline, therapy can help you calm your nervous system and restore a sense of safety.

Questions: What do I do when I feel like I'm not making progress?
Answers: Progress is often invisible in the moment because it happens in small increments. Look back over the last few months and list changes, even tiny ones. Growth is rarely a straight line; plateaus are part of it. If you're truly stuck, get specific: what one small next step could you take? Progress starts with showing up again.

Questions: How can I help myself feel safer?
Answers: Feeling safe starts with your body: slow breathing, grounding, and steady routines create calm signals. Identify what makes you feel unsafe and reduce exposure to it where you can. Keep people and places that feel safe close. If the lack of safety is rooted in trauma, trauma-informed therapy can help you rebuild a genuine sense of safety over time.

Questions: What helps with feeling like I'm always apologizing?
Answers: Notice when you apologize for things that aren't your fault, and pause before it. Practice replacing 'sorry' with 'thank you' where it fits, like 'thanks for waiting' instead of 'sorry I'm late.' You're allowed to take up space without shrinking. Self-worth work can help you feel entitled to time, space, and kindness.

Questions: How can I handle uncertainty?
Answers: Anchor yourself in what's stable: routines, values, and people. Break big unknowns into next steps you can take. Practice sitting with 'maybe' without needing an immediate answer. You've lived with uncertainty before and found your way through. You can again, and support can help you build that tolerance.

Questions: What should I do when I feel like I've lost myself?
Answers: Reconnect with what you value, enjoy, and believe. Try small things that used to feel like you, and see what resonates now. Identity can be rebuilt, and it's allowed to evolve. You're not gone; you're becoming. With patience and support, you can find your way back to yourself, one small authentic choice at a time.

Questions: How can I stop feeling like a failure?
Answers: Feeling like a failure is a story, not a fact. Make a list of things you've accomplished and survived, even small ones. Reframe failures as learning and redirection. You're not defined by outcomes; you're defined by your effort and character. If this feeling is persistent, therapy can help you rewrite the story and see yourself accurately.

Questions: I don't know if I have depression, but I have been very sad. There are nights that I don't sleep. I don't eat all day sometimes, I don't have energy to anything anymore.
Answers: These. symptoms are all classic to the diagnosis of depression.A diagnosis itself doesn't help anyone get better. Often people say the word \depression\" as though it means something terrible. The diagnosis of depression can be depressing.Forget matching symptoms with a diagnosis.More important to improvement is to know the reason for your sadness. When people become sad there is a reason for it and knowing this reason is the first step to changing the situation which creates the sadness in you.Think of depression as a way to slow down and examine aspects of your life and relationships. If you continue at the same pace of living and didn't stop and examine your life

Questions: I'm currently up paranoid about, well, everything. I can't get to sleep, and I have a feeling of being watched constantly. I have extreme depression and anxiety. I'd really like to not be this paranoid and go to bed. I've tried night lights, ambiance, and warm baths.
Answers: What kinds of things help you to feel safe? I think it's great you've already tried a few things to help yourself sleep, even if they don't work. Those methods of coping could be targeting something other than paranoia--which is maybe why you aren't finding those things are helpful. If you are really struggling, sometimes meds can help to calm the brain a bit. If you choose this route, make sure you give your prescribing doctor all the information about your symptoms so your meds can be as accurate as possible for what you're dealing with.If you have access, counseling could be beneficial as well. There are more and more counselors becoming available via telehealth because of COVID, so you could even find someone to help you right in the space you feel most paranoid about (given that space is private). Either way, talking some of those fears through could at the very least bring some insight, if not some relief.

Questions: I have an alcoholic son who is draining me financially. I want to get him help, but he doesn't want help. It's making me anxious and depressed.
Answers: What a heavy situation to be in. It must be really hard to feel like you aren't able to help your son and the help you do try to give isn't truly helping him or you. There's some things in this situation that are out of your control--what your son does, if he takes help or doesn't, and the feelings that come up for you about that. I can only imagine how draining it would be as a parent to be unable to change something so important. It makes sense you'd be feeling anxious and depressed.Let's switch for a minute to the things you have total control over--what are those things in this situation? Maybe that's how you express your love for your son. Or maybe it's how you choose to support him (even if it feels like it's a betrayal to him). Pay attention as well to the amount of worry you experience--how much of that helps you plan vs how much of that is excess? Knowing what worry isn't necessary can help to put you in control of how you spend some of your time. You can replace this time with some self-care instead, giving back to yourself.Finding support groups or people that have similar situations can be very helpful. I'd say they are almost necessary. Knowing other people get what you are going through and understand the emotional toll can be somewhat healing. They may also know other resources or ideas you can try that are available to people in your situation.Something else to consider is grief work. Letting go of some or all of the situation with your son (if that's what it comes down to) is a giant loss. You probably already went through losing who your son was before the addiction, so it could be worth exploring the impact that had and has on you.

Questions: I think adult life is making him depressed and we often sleep in on weekends untill 1 or 2 pm. We just eat, smoke weed, watch movies, and he'll go on his phone all day. He doesn't seem motivated to do much and he's often angry.\n I have no clue how to help him take his mind off the negative, or to distract him into a different light. How do I help him?
Answers: That's a giant task to have to do all on your own. It's hard to watch someone you care about feel depressed and I'm guessing it brings you down, too. Change is tricky. Most people need to hit a \rock bottom\" before they can transform their lives. Rock bottom is a moving target though--meaning one person's rock bottom could look completely different than someone else's. For some people that's a trip to the hospital

Questions: She has trouble falling and staying asleep and she's always either extremely hungry or not hungry at all. She also gets angry and feels like crying really easily for no reason. She says she is always \kind of down.\"\n Is this depression? What can I do to help her?"
Answers: Do you feel heavy with despair, struggling each day to keep your head just above the darkness and dread? Does it take every ounce of energy to stay afloat? Or are you feeling overwhelmed by feelings of helplessness and hopelessness? If this sounds familiar, we want you to know that you are not alone and therapy for depression could help.While it may seem difficult to find your way back to hope and happiness, therapists have been helping clients to personally do just that for years. To experience the joy of warm sunshine on their face, to reconnect with estranged loved ones, and to re-engage with a meaningful life.Just like other chronic illnesses, depression is not your fault, it’s nothing you’ve caused. And also like many other illnesses, effective treatments exist to help ease and eliminate the struggles you face.If you’ve said or thought these things a lot recently: “I’m too tired to try.”“I don’t want to leave home.”“I don’t care anymore.”“Why am I always crying?”“I don’t even know who I am any more.” Or even, “I wish I wasn’t here.” Then there are proven steps and therapies that can help you get remarkable relief. Therapy for depression can bring you hope, help and a way forward. Visit denvermhc.com to read more.

Questions: I'm a teenager and I I go through periods of moodiness. I have extreme feelings (but I bury them), and then I feel nothing - just empty and emotionless.\n I have trust issues, low self esteem,ban extreme fear of abandonment, and I constantly reevaluate my relationships. I also don't know who I am as a person. I'm not happy overall, but I'm not suicidal. Can I just feel happy?
Answers: Sometimes the way to feel happy is to address all the questions you just described.Teenage years are the first time any of us starts to feel and recognize our uniqueness. The fact that you recognize your great range of feelings, as uncomfortable as they may sometimes be, is healthy.Also healthy is that you are asking for opinions of therapists who would be familiar with when a range of feelings shows an out of the ordinary problem.One path to take is to reflect on the topics you wrote here and especially to ask yourself your reasons for how the problem started and what it would take for it to resolve.Do you have trust issues because someone broke your trust? You're entitled to a repair of your trust by the other person. Even if the person never offers this to you, to know you deserve to be restored to whole, may help you feel more secure.The same is true with the other topics, abandonment and relationships generally.The more you continue to value your unique understanding, expectations, and standards, the more likely you'll create relationships which do not have these qualities, and you will restore your sense of hope that other people may treat you in a fair and kind way.

Questions: I've been having this ongoing problem for most of my life now. I am a young adult, and right now, driving and even being a passenger gives me terrible panic attacks and anxiety. I can't ride in the backseat or the front seat with the safety belt on. I have to lean the seat back a bit because the pressure on my back terrifies me. I miss so many opportunities to go places with friends and family because of my fears of having a panic attack. My family offers little to no support. They think it's fake or \all in my head.\" It makes me feel guilty and at times depressed to the point where I'd rather never wake up anymore. I am not self-harming
Answers: Sherry Katz, LCSWCouples and Family Therapist, LCSW

Questions: My fiancée suffers from severe anxiety and depression. She has had it most of her life. Her anxiety in public places is the worst. It gets to points where she can't breathe or move. Sometimes, she won't even go to the restroom, so she will hold in her pee until her stomach hurts or she pees herself. She curls up in corners at the mall and has panic attacks. She won't eat or drink in public. If she isn't having a panic attack or crying, she's clinging to me and avoiding everything and everyone. Her depression flares up out of nowhere and causes her to become very suicidal and self-harming. She get really sick from anxiety and scared to the point that I can't even get her to eat, drink, leave the bed, or go outside. She always tells me how she grew up around so much fighting and fear that it makes her scared of loud sounds, yelling, conflict, and even talking to strangers in public. She will refuse to go to a store unless I am with her to talk to the cashier for her. She is so scared that I can't even get her to drive. She doesn't want to get her license because she's scared of trying to drive.\n Some people have recommended medication, but I believe it's just going to cover up her illness and not solve it. I don't want my fiancée pumped with drugs. I believe a psychiatric service dog would be the best bet for her. When we first met my poodle, it would calm her down a lot. She took the dog out every time we went out, and she seemed much calmer and happier. She slowly would eat, and the dog seemed to make her feel a lot better. I am worried and want to help her without medication.
Answers: It sounds like you have been a positive support for your fiancee. There is no doubt that this situation is a great challenge for the both of you. While it may feel like you are responsible for her health and happiness, it is important that you understand that you, on your own, won't be able to resolve her mental health issues. Based on what you have explained, it sounds like she needs to get a medical and/or psychiatric evaluation. Whether or not she decides to take medication is her (and your) decision, but keeping an open mind about treatment options is important. I suggest that she see a therapist on her own in order to better understand and cope with her anxiety and depression, especially given her suicidal thoughts. You would also likely benefit from therapy, individual or couple's therapy, in order to address how you are feeling and best learn how to support her and your relationship. I wish the very best for both of you and hope that things will improve sooner than later.

Questions: My last relationships have ended horribly. They just up and abandoned me. One of them I have never gotten closure with over it, leaving me emotionally wrecked. I know something's wrong with me but I don't know how to even start trying to better myself.\n I get into these depressed like states whenever anyone I care about is too busy to be with me. I know that I shouldn't act like that because people are genuinely busy, but I feel like they're doing it just because they don't want to be around me.
Answers: Frequently when working with clients, I utilize the A-B-C model developed by Albert Ellis, the founder of Rational Emotive Behavior Theory. The theory basically states that you can not control an event but you can control your reaction to the emotions associated with said event. For instance here is an example:A (Action or Event): You need to talk to someone and that person is not calling you back.B (Behavior or Response): You begin to tell yourself that this person is too busy for me or I am not important to this person.C (Consequence): You feel depressed.If you look at the model, B has a direct effect on C. The thought is if you change your reaction to A, then C will have a better consequence, such as:A: stays the same.B (this is what you change): This person must be busy, they will call me back when they get a chance or I can call someone else to lean on for support until this person is available.C: Decreased feelings of depression & overall functioning improves.This is just an example but if you actively work to replace the negative thought patterns that effect your behavior, studies show that your overall outlook and mood will improve. If this model resonates with you, I recommend \Feeling better

Questions: When I get frustrated or upset, it becomes extremely difficult to keep my voice down. I also instantly cry and tend to have anxiety attacks. What can I do to try and control it?
Answers: I'm going to reframe this and you can decide if this is helpful!What I'm reading based on what you gave is that you are actually doing your best to manage intense feelings of internal dysregulation. Anger is something that is generally a protective emotion that quickly arises to keep us safe in some way, whether or not the situation is truly a threat. The part of our brain that perceives this is not controllable to us, so we don't get to decide what emotion(s) we respond with.It does also sound like you are experiencing some significant anxiety, maybe even underlying the anger? Without knowing the context, it's hard to say what would help on an individual level but working through those triggers and what is really influencing them deep down could be beneficial. There's many different ways to do that in therapy if you so choose that as your path.If you do decide to see a therapist, most will tell you that the goal is not necessarily to control your anxiety or anger. Sometimes there's a strong set of beliefs that, when activated, are catalysts to strong emotions that influence behavior. Trying to control an emotion on its own is usually unsuccessful for people because it leaves out all the other powerful elements at play. Emotions are information and the brain sends that information out because it believes we need it at that time. Therapists can help unravel that with you in whatever way you need, whether that's with somatic work, work at the level of belief (or schemas), or otherwise---hitting it at these deeper layers can unpair and/or decrease emotional responses. It all takes work and time, so don't get down on yourself if the process is complicated or slower than you expected or hoped for.What we know though is that the brain is very capable of change (even if it's painful). Hope this gives you a helpful place to start from!

Questions: My two adult sons live with me. One has been having panic attacks and hasn't been able to work for over 6 months. He doesn't want to get help. I'm feeling so overwhelmed. What can I do?
Answers: My very first thought is this is so much to carry on your own! A mother's instinct is to care for her children so I can imagine how hard it must be to see your son in pain and struggling. I hear a ping of helplessness in there as well. That's heavy.My question is: who is supporting you? I know nothing about the context, but I wonder if the role you hold often is that of caretaker. It may not be that the end-all-be-all answer is to be cared for, but the absence of care (or even self-care) can seem like we are only existing for others. Sometimes having someone to rely on can help take off some of the edge--the pressure--of all that is overwhelming.Despite that, it may be that the situation continues to be exactly what it is, providing a steady stream of stress for you (which would be so difficult). I don't think anyone can tell you what to do because no one here has to live with those consequences, good or bad. Just a note that sometimes with men it is harder to reach out for help. Perhaps he feels comfortable enough for you to know he's struggling (which means you have provided him a safe space to do just that) but not comfortable enough to interact with a stranger about those same struggles. Men often avoid therapy because it's seen as weak and/or means you need help. Planting seeds here is sometimes all you can do, as hard as that is.As far as supporting goes, there's much more you can do there if he is ready to receive that. If you are seeing him in the midst of panic, the best thing you can do is let him know you are there for him. Maybe that means being there physically, or continuing to give him encouragement along the way (e.g., \You got this\"

Questions: I have developed bad social anxiety within the last year, and I just can't stand to be around people. I recently got a new girlfriend, and she is extremely close to her large family and wants me to be around them all of the time. My last visit with them, I was quiet and uncomfortable, and she got mad.
Answers: Take small steps each day. Go around a few people, take a walk, and smile or wave at others. Strike up a conversation in the grocery aisle. Think of topics you enjoy and would like to share, could talk about, to break the ice. Maybe call some friends you once had and reconnect. Go at a pace that feels comfortable and in time you could release the reclusive energy to embrace a more social you. I also wanted to share this short digital book with you. The Anxiety Antidote

Questions: I have a friend who I became quite close to, close enough for us to insult each other lightly for humor. But eventually, that went too far. Recently, I've realized that it is causing me lots of stress and anxiety. I can't get away because I fell in love with them.
Answers: Sending you positive vibes as you contend with loving someone who bullies you. Have you discussed how this leads you to feel and if they can stop? Open honest communication is a key cornerstone in relationships. Take away the bullying and list the other qualities about them you love. Also, write down the pros and cons of staying versus leaving. If possible dig into what leads you to love someone who bullies you? Were you bullied by someone you love in the past and this resonates because it is familiar? Also please journal if you wish around the graphic enclosed.

Questions: My son was diagnosed with autism a few years ago and I stopped working so that I could take care of him. I also was dealing with an abusive relationship (mentally, physically, and emotionally). Now I live like a recluse and I always feel nervous around people.\n How can I feel more comfortable around other people?
Answers: There's a lot of layers there to your situation, and I'm focusing on two layers that may be contributing to your feelings of discomfort around others. One layer is the daunting news that your son has autism. Many parents can feel overwhelmed and distraught with this diagnosis. The vast array of treatments available is daunting in and of itself at times to wrap one's head around. Taking time to reflect or seek out therapy regarding how this diagnosis has impacted you may be helpful. Some parents feel their individual identity gets lost in the diagnosis because they have dropped everything to help their child, and others may experience guilt. If either of these or other feelings come to the forefront for you, it may be worth working through them with a therapist. A support group list is available through www.autismspeaks.org and may help connect you with others raising children with autism.A second layer is the abusive relationship you were involved in. The trauma you experienced in this relationship may have a very meaningful impact on your ability to trust and to be intimate with others. Engaging with a therapist can help facilitate the healing process, as well as paving the way for more comfortable and trusting relationships.

Questions: I recently broke up with my boyfriend After being together for over 4 years. I truly believe I did the right thing, but omehow being single now has made me very needy and unsure of myself.\n I am seeing someone casually and I am losing my mind with anxiety about how he feels about me and this need for validation.\n How can I learn to be content and at peace with myself regardless of my career, relationship status, etc?
Answers: Possibly you haven't completed your phase of mourning the recently passed relationship and lifestyle which surrounded it.Relationship breakups mean a person's entire life goes through an adjustment since the relationship impacted all areas of your life.Give yourself some patience to restore yourself from the old relationship. When you feel whole again then more than likely you will lose some of the anxiety wondering what your new casual partner feels about you.And instead of wondering, you may simply decide to ask the person your question!
